title: Computer-Use 2.0: Agents Just Got Multi-Cursor — Francesco Bonacci, Cua

summary: The presentation spans three speakers. Francesco Bonacci introduces cua driver, a background computer-use tool that replaces the old screenshot-based agent loop (computer use 1.0) with direct communication to undocumented OS accessibility APIs. This lets agents interact with background or hidden windows without stealing focus. The driver first attempts accessibility-tree-based execution, falling back to pixel-level background clicks. It was built in one weekend after Codex released its computer use model and works across macOS, Windows, and Linux. Eight application harnesses guard against regressions. CTO Dylan presents CUABench, their evaluation framework with setup/oracle/evaluator structure and a single-file Python SDK. The benchmark includes 130+ tasks across 42 environments and five platforms. The Snorkel AI collaboration on electrical engineering tasks using real professional software with circuit-simulating evaluators produced humbling results: the best agent passed only 6 of 25 tasks (all editing existing schematics), 0% from blank schematics, no model above 30% reward. On the basic 4K dataset, switching from a standard tool to cua driver raised pass rates from 62% to 80% while using 34% fewer tokens, primarily because cua driver monitors a single window. Before any task enters the dataset, a matrix of agents attempts reward hacking; only surviving tasks are admitted. World models are measured by forking trajectories and probing models to predict state. Chief Infra Officer Rob addresses GPU idle time during RL training, where sandbox startup and reset cycles waste expensive GPU time. His demand-based autoscaler dynamically sizes a warm sandbox pool to match GPU cluster needs; since sandboxes cost 2-4x less than GPUs, redundancy still saves money. Instant sandboxes are available for Windows, Linux, Android, and macOS (coming). In Q&A, Francesco addresses Android support: the team works with ARM's team on an harness for Android, where some background operation is possible through containerized workloads, but Android background computer use leans more toward tool use via the activity framework than full GUI control.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

Cua Fleet provides instant sandboxes for Windows, Linux, Android, and macOS (coming) for GPU-based RL training.

sections.title: Introduction and Vision of Cua
sections.summary: Francesco introduces himself and team members Dylan and Rob, surveys audience familiarity with computer-use agents, and describes computer use 1.0: an old-fashioned human-agent loop using screenshots, reasoning, and click/type/scroll action space.

sections.title: Overview of Cua Driver and Background Operation
sections.summary: Francesco explains cua driver: a background computer-use tool built in one weekend after Codex's release, using undocumented OS accessibility APIs (AX on macOS, UI Automation on Windows, AT-SPI on Linux) to let agents act without stealing focus. Agents snapshot window state, try accessibility-tree execution, fall back to pixel background clicks. Eight application harnesses prevent regressions.

sections.title: Introduction to Cua Bench and Agent Evaluation
sections.summary: CTO Dylan presents CUABench: 130+ verifiable tasks across 42 environments and 5 platforms with setup/oracle/evaluator structure. Snorkel AI collaboration on EE tasks showed best agent passing 6/25 (all editing existing schematics, 0% on blank, no model above 30% reward). Switching to cua driver raised 4K benchmark from 62% to 80% with 34% fewer tokens. Reward-hacking matrix tests tasks before admission. World models measured via trajectory forking.

sections.title: Cua Fleet and GPU Infrastructure Optimization
sections.summary: Chief Infra Officer Rob addresses GPU idle time during RL training for computer-use agents. Sandbox startup and reset waste expensive GPU time. Solution: demand-based autoscaler dynamically sizes warm sandbox pool to match GPU needs. Sandboxes 2-4x cheaper than GPUs, so redundancy still saves money by maximizing GPU utilization. Instant sandboxes available for Windows, Linux, Android, and macOS (coming).

sections.title: Q&A Session
sections.summary: Francesco opens Q&A covering cua driver, CUABench, and cua fleet. Asked about Android support, he explains the team works with ARM's team on an Android harness; background operation on Android is possible through containerized workloads but leans toward tool use via the activity framework rather than full GUI control. The Android ecosystem is more inclined to background computer use than iOS.
